title: Controlling Atom Array in an Ultra-high-cooperativity Optical Cavity
authors: Jilai Ye, Zhihao Chi, Ye Tian, Shuyao Mei, Xiaoyu Li, Wenjun Zhang, Yajuan Zhao, Jiazhong Hu, Wenlan Chen
abstract: Neutral-atom array and cavity quantum electrodynamics offer complementary strengths for quantum science: scalable, reconfigurable qubit architectures and strong coherent light-matter coupling. Combining them in a single platform requires an optical cavity with simultaneously high cooperativity, sufficient mode volume to accommodate atom array, and ample side optical access for atom trapping, imaging, cooling, and rearrangement, a combination that is challenging to achieve. Here we realize an atomic array integrated with a millimeter-scale Fabry--Pérot cavity whose optically-characterized single-atom cooperativity reaches $η_{\mathrm{cav}}=125\pm13$. Atom-cavity transmission spectra of trapped atoms yield an effective spectroscopic cooperativity $η_{\mathrm{spec}}=112.3\pm3.3$, providing an in-situ verification of strong coupling in the integrated platform, and we demonstrate simultaneous coupling of up to 16 individually trapped atoms to the antinode of the cavity mode. The key technical advance is a two-step mirror-fabrication method combining precision mechanical shaping and carbon-dioxide laser polishing, which produces concave fused-silica mirrors with sub-millimeter radii of curvature and residual roughness below 2 Å. Our results establish a regime of cavity-integrated atomic array that simultaneously provides high cooperativity, large mode volume, and flexible manipulation of individual atoms, opening opportunities for cavity-assisted quantum state readout and long-range entanglement-engineering in atom-array platforms.
summary: The research reports the creation of an integrated platform combining neutral-atom arrays with a high-finesse Fabry-Pérot cavity. By developing novel mirror fabrication techniques, they achieved strong single-atom coupling ($\eta_{	ext{cav}} \approx 125$) while maintaining the large mode volume necessary for trapping many atoms. This opens pathways for complex quantum simulations involving collective atomic interactions mediated by light.
main_problem: The challenge is integrating neutral-atom arrays, which offer scalable qubit architectures, with high-cooperativity optical cavities, which provide strong light-matter coupling.
main_result: The authors successfully realized an integrated platform achieving a single-atom cooperativity of $\eta_{	ext{cav}}=125\pm13$ while maintaining large mode volume compatible with trapping up to 16 individual atoms.
method: They employed a two-step mirror fabrication process and characterized the system by measuring atom-cavity transmission spectra as the number of trapped atoms was varied.
model_or_system: The platform consists of an atomic array (e.g., Rb-87) coupled to a millimeter-scale Fabry-Pérot cavity, enabling controlled interaction between individual atoms and the cavity mode.
key_observables: Single-atom cooperativity ($\eta_{	ext{cav}}$), effective spectroscopic cooperativity ($\eta_{	ext{spec}}$), and atom-cavity transmission spectra as a function of trapped atom number ($N$).
important_parameters: High cooperativity regime ($\eta \approx 100$), millimeter-scale cavity size, sub-2 Å mirror roughness, and the ability to couple up to 16 atoms simultaneously.
main_assumptions: The difference between measured $\eta_{	ext{spec}}$ and theoretical $\eta_{	ext{cav}}$ is attributed to spatial spreading of atoms or placement errors within the lattice.
figures_summary: Figure 3 shows atom-cavity transmission spectra, demonstrating the measurable spectroscopic cooperativity ($\eta_{	ext{spec}}$) for varying numbers of trapped atoms ($N=1$ through $N=16$).
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the need to combine scalable atomic arrays with high-cooperativity cavities. It details the advanced hardware fabrication techniques, presents measurements confirming strong coupling ($\eta_{	ext{cav}}$), and finally demonstrates in-situ characterization by measuring $\eta_{	ext{spec}}$ across multiple trapped atoms.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a major engineering hurdle in quantum simulation: creating large, controllable arrays of qubits (atoms) that are strongly coupled to high-quality optical cavities for advanced quantum state manipulation and entanglement generation.
